A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ResearchTown, TextGNN and ResearchBench. Their text, equations, tables, figures and appendices are readable, and corresponding content can be matched despite extensive reformatting and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original paper-writing and review-writing simulations, neighborhood ablations, high-impact-paper evaluations and interdisciplinary case studies.

after.justification: v2 retains original simulation results and adds generation-model comparisons, LLM-based assessments and human evaluation.

M1.justification: The agent-data graph, TextGNN message passing, three research activities and efficient aggregation procedure remain substantively unchanged. Expanded descriptions of inputs, structured outputs and length control clarify procedures already represented in v1's appendix prompts.

E1.justification: Both retain 1,000 paper-writing tasks, 200 review-writing tasks, 100 high-impact papers and the same interdisciplinary cases. The human study samples existing PAPERBENCH outputs; additional calibration examples and model configurations remain within the existing research-paper and review tasks.

E2.justification: Self-, Agent-, Data- and Global-agg are retained as AGG-self, AGG-agent, AGG-data and AGG-global. Qwen and DeepSeek are additional backbones tested with these same strategies, rather than new competing simulation algorithms. ResearchAgent is cited but not experimentally compared.

E3.justification: v2 adds Qwen-2.5-7B-Instruct and DeepSeek-v3 configurations, GPT-4o evaluation across six similarity dimensions, novelty/feasibility assessments, and a 40-pair human evaluation with two annotators. It also reports mean review ratings and drops NV-Embed-v2 evaluation reporting. Existing benchmark sizes, difficulty splits and temperature-zero GPT-4o-mini settings are retained.

E4.justification: Sections 9–10 and Appendix F add model-family sensitivity tests, fine-grained consistency and intrinsic-quality analyses, human validation, and real-world similarity calibration. These substantially broaden v1's neighborhood ablations and case studies. The high-impact-paper analysis is largely relocated, not newly introduced.

E5.justification: v2 introduces Pearson correlation analysis of human–LLM agreement, reporting 0.61 for similarity and qualitatively low agreement for intrinsic quality. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals or significance tests for the benchmark comparisons.

E6.justification: Table 1 revises GPT-4o-mini overall paper-writing scores: global aggregation changes from 67.28 to 67.51, data from 66.72 to 65.30, agent from 54.61 to 55.24, and self from 43.65 to 46.08. Paper-ablation values also change. v2 adds extensive cross-model, judge, human and calibration results, while removing detailed NV-Embed-v2 and Voyage paper-score breakdowns and the reviewer-weakness ablation series. These are reported result changes, not demonstrated improvements from a revised method.

T1.justification: The graph definitions, substantive message-passing equations and paper/review similarity definitions are retained. Equations are reformatted and renumbered, and metric definitions move to Appendix F. No new theorem, proof, formal assumption or substantive derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: Both versions claim a unified graph/TextGNN research-community simulator, similarity-based ResearchBench evaluation, robust collaborative simulation and interdisciplinary ideation. Revised numerical summaries and additional supporting evaluations do not materially redefine these central contributions.

C2.justification: v2 discusses shortcomings of aggregate cosine similarity, weak human–LLM agreement on intrinsic quality, and possible training-data exposure for high-impact papers. It corrects v1's statement that global aggregation decreases review-score discrepancies and introduces a model-dependent explanation. Appendices also expand the interpretation and applicability of the evaluation framework.

D1.justification: v2 documents API variants and licenses for the added generators, supplies the evaluation prompt in Table 17, and describes human annotators, sampling and annotation calibration in Appendix H. It also explains output-length control. Existing generation prompts, dataset-construction procedures and code/data access links remain largely intact.

R1.justification: v2 adds ResearchAgent to the introduction and Chen et al. (2025) and Jin et al. (2025) as examples for similarity calibration; the bibliography also adds Langley (2000). Positioning against text-attributed graphs and graph-based multi-agent research remains substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: detailed metric definitions move to Appendix F, high-impact results move to Appendix J, and licenses become a separate Artifact appendix. Method explanations expand, ablation discussion is reorganized, and case-study and conclusion prose is condensed. New evaluation and impact sections further change the document structure.

P2.justification: The main text changes from single-column to two-column layout. Tables 1–2 are redesigned, new comparison and quality tables and a judge-evaluation figure appear, and appendix result tables are substantially restructured. The high-impact histogram disappears, while the reviewer ablation changes plotted metrics and axes. Existing prompt and case-study tables are retained with resizing and renumbering.

improvement.justification: v2 improves evidential support beyond v1's embedding-based evaluation through additional backbones, explicit quality assessments and a 40-pair human check. However, new reporting inconsistencies limit the gain: Section 9's DeepSeek-over-GPT ranking conflicts with Table 3, and GPT-4o-mini's review-score difference is 1.51 there versus 1.55 in Tables 2 and 6. The broader validation is useful, but the small human study and inconsistent reporting prevent a clear substantial improvement.
